Theodōrus autem nōn ībat sed currēbat — Theo, though, wasn’t walking but running (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Theodōrus autem, in umerīs ejus vectus, bacillum aduncum tenēns — Theo, riding on his shoulders and holding his hooked stick (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
tolūtim — at a trot (Traupman 60; Varro; Pliny); tolūtim currere / cursitāre — trot, jog.

ad olīvam tolūtim cucurrit truncumque manū tangēns «Valē, olīva!» inquit — he trotted over to the olive tree and, touching the trunk, said, “Goodbye, olive tree!” (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

english: Swimming pool / swim / float / dive / bubbles / chlorine
keywords: pool swimming swim float dive diving underwater bubbles chlorine chlorinated

items.html: piscīna, piscīnae f. — swimming pool (Traupman 50); originally a fishpond, a bathing pool from the first century AD, as in Pliny’s heated pool: cohaeret calida piscīna mīrifica, ex quā natantēs mare aspiciunt — “next to it is a wonderful heated pool, from which swimmers look out at the sea” (Plin. Ep. 2.17.11).

natō, natāre, natāvī, natātum — swim; also float, as Cato’s test for brine: sī natābit, “if it floats” (Agr. 88). Pliny’s rule for a river: īnfrā etiam natāre concessum, “downstream you may swim too” (Ep. 8.8.6).
innatō, innatāre — float on, swim in (poetic and post-Augustan prose, L&S); innatāns of the dishes floating round the edge of Pliny’s garden pool (Ep. 5.6.37).

ūrīnor, ūrīnārī — dive, go under water (Varro, L.L. 5.126; Pliny); ūrīnātor, ūrīnātōris m. — diver (M-O s.v. diver). For jumping in head first, see the Jump / dive in headfirst entry: praeceps dēsiliō.
bulla, bullae f. — bubble (Ov. Met. 10.734).

chlōrium, chlōriī n. — chlorine (M-O s.v. chlorine, a modern coinage; Traupman has none). aqua chlōrāta — chlorinated water; aqua sine chlōriō — water without chlorine. Both phrases are our formations.
Vīsne natāre? — Do you want to swim?
Ecce, bullae! — Look, bubbles!
Nōlō tē nimis diū in aquā chlōrātā manēre. — I don’t want you staying too long in the chlorinated water.

english: Massage / rub down / masseur / oil / relax
keywords: massage massages masseur masseuse massage therapist back rub shoulders oil relax

items.html: fricō, fricāre, fricuī, frictum — rub, rub down, massage (M-O s.v. massage); fricārī — have a massage, be rubbed down: numquam concessāmus lavārī aut fricārī aut tergērī aut ōrnārī — “we never stopped being bathed, rubbed down, dried and dressed” (Plaut. Poen. 219–220).

frictiō, frictiōnis f.; fricātiō, fricātiōnis f. — a rub-down, massage (Celsus, who gives it a chapter, 2.14). After a long walk: hunc reficit in ipsō quoque itinere frequēns frictiō, post iter prīmum sedīle, deinde ūnctiō — “he is restored by frequent rubbing on the way, and after the walk first a seat, then an oiling” (Cels. 1.3).
malaxō, malaxāre — knead, soften, massage (M-O s.v. massage, citing Seneca, Ep. 66.53, where it is scornful, of pampered luxury).

iātralīptēs, iātralīptae m. — massage therapist, a doctor who treats with oil and rubbing. Pliny asked Trajan for citizenship for his own: gravissimā valētūdine ūsque ad perīculum vītae vexātus iātralīptēn assūmpsī — “when a very serious illness put my life in danger, I took on a massage therapist” (Plin. Ep. 10.5.1).

tractātor, tractātōris m.; tractātrīx, tractātrīcis f. — masseur, masseuse (Sen. Ep. 66.53; Mart. 3.82.13), both in scornful passages; M-O s.v. masseur gives fricātor and, with a query, tractātor. alīptēs, alīptae m. — the trainer who oiled and rubbed down athletes (Cic. Fam. 1.9.15); ūnctor, ūnctōris m. — anointer (Cic., Mart.).
oleum, oleī n. — oil; ungō (unguō), ungere, ūnxī, ūnctum — rub with oil; ūnctiō, ūnctiōnis f. — oiling; unguentum, unguentī n. — ointment, scented oil.
animum relaxāre; sē ex labōre relaxāre — relax, unwind (M-O s.v. relax); quiēscere — rest.
Fricā mihi tergum, quaesō. — Rub my back, please.
Vīsne ut tibi umerōs fricem? — Shall I rub your shoulders?
Pedēs tibi oleō ungam. — I’ll rub your feet with oil.
Ah, quam bene est! — Ah, that feels good!

blocks.html: Quantities of the Greek loans follow the Greek: iātralīptēs (ἰᾱτραλείπτης), alīptēs (ἀλείπτης). ūnctor, ūnctiō, ūnxī and ūnctum have the long vowel before -nct-/-nx-.

english: Herbal remedies: herbal tea / infusion / decoction / poultice / compress / honey / chamomile / mint / thyme / sage / linden / nettle
latin: īnfūsum, īnfūsī n. · dēcoctum, dēcoctī n. · fōmentum, fōmentī n.
keywords: herbal tea herb tea tisane infusion decoction steep brew remedy home remedy natural remedy poultice compress hot compress cold compress honey chamomile camomile mint peppermint thyme sage linden lime blossom lime flower nettle sore throat gargle cough

items.html: īnfūsum, īnfūsī n. — herbal tea, infusion, with the genitive of the herb: īnfūsum chamaemēlī, īnfūsum mentae (M-O s.v. tea: herb tea, citing 19th-century pharmacy Latin, e.g. infūsum flōrum chamomillae; a Neo-Latin noun from īnfundō, īnfundere, īnfūdī, īnfūsum, pour in). M-O’s distinction: an infusion is boiling water poured over the herb and left to stand; a decoction is boiled with the herb in it. Traupman has no herb tea; he gives only thea (the tea entry).

dēcoquō, dēcoquere, dēcoxī, dēcoctum — boil down, boil (a herb) in water; dēcoctum, dēcoctī n. — decoction, the liquid so made (Pliny; M-O s.v. tea: herb tea, decoctum with the genitive). Pliny’s wild poppy melle dēcoctum ad faucium remedia, “boiled with honey, a remedy for the throat” (Plin. NH 18.229), and hyssop: hȳsōpī fasciculus cum quadrante mellis dēcoquitur ad tussim — “a bunch of hyssop is boiled with a quarter-pound of honey for a cough” (Plin. NH 26.31).

fōmentum, fōmentī n. — compress, warm application, fomentation (from foveō); fōmenta calida / frīgida. Celsus: fōmenta quoque calida sunt milium, sāl, harēna, quidlibet eōrum calfactum et in linteum conjectum — “warm compresses are millet, salt, sand, any of them heated and put in a cloth” (Cels. 2.17). Horace’s friend at the bedside assideat, fōmenta paret, medicum roget (Serm. 1.1.82). foveō, fovēre, fōvī, fōtum — bathe, soak a sore limb (Traupman 61–62: fovē illud genū in aquā frīgidā).

cataplasma, cataplasmatis n. — poultice (Celsus, Pliny; Greek κατάπλασμα); Celsus’s linseed poultice softens: praecipueque ad ēmolliendum potest cataplasma ex līnī vel fēnī Graecī sēmine (Cels. 2.33). malagma, malagmatis n. — softening poultice (Celsus).

mel, mellis n. — honey; mel cum aquā calidā — honey in hot water; hydromeli, hydromelitis n. — honey-water (Pliny). For a sore throat Celsus has you boil thyme or hyssop and gargle: hȳsōpum vel nepetam vel thumum … dēcoquere, eaque gargarīzāre (Cels. 4.7, on a swollen throat; the edition spells thumum). gargarīzō, gargarīzāre — gargle (Cels., Plin.; M-O s.v. gargle).

chamaemēlon, chamaemēlī n. — chamomile (Plin. NH 22.53, who explains the name: chamaemēlon, quoniam odōrem mālī habeat, “because it smells of apples”; M-O s.v. chamomile). Also anthemis, anthemidis f. (Pliny’s main headword) and the later chamomilla (Plin. Val.).

menta (mentha), mentae f. — mint (Ov., Plin.); menta piperāta — peppermint (M-O, pharmacy Latin); M-O’s own example is mentae īnfūsum, mint tea. Pliny: mentae ipsīus odor animum excitat — “the very smell of mint revives the spirit” (NH 20.147).
thymum, thymī n. — thyme (Verg., Hor., Plin.); serpyllum, serpyllī n. — wild thyme (Cato, Varro, Verg.), the kind on the hillsides above the village. Bulgarian мащерка.
salvia, salviae f. — sage (Plin. NH 22.147, giving the Greek elelisphacum).

tilia, tiliae f. — linden, lime tree (see the forest trees entry); īnfūsum flōrum tiliae — linden-blossom tea, Bulgarian липов чай, is our formation on M-O’s pattern. Pliny knows linden bark for swellings and wounds (NH 24.49), not the blossom tea.

urtīca, urtīcae f. — nettle (Catull., Hor., Plin.); Pliny opens his chapter Urtīcā quid esse invīsius potest? at illa … vel plūrimīs scatet remediīs — “what could be more hateful than the nettle? yet it teems with remedies” (NH 22.31). For Catullus’s cold cured ōtiōque et urtīcā see the Common cold entry.

unguentum, unguentī n. — ointment, salve (see the massage entry); linīmentum, linīmentī n. — lotion, liniment (Traupman 64; M-O s.v. ointment, late: Palladius, Caelius Aurelianus); cērātum, cērātī n. — wax salve (Cels.). illinō, illinere, illēvī, illitum — smear on; M-O’s infricāre — rub in (Plin.).
remedium, remediī n. — remedy, with genitive or ad: remedium tussis / ad tussim (Traupman 370; Cic.); herbae medicae — medicinal herbs.
Īnfūsum tibi chamaemēlī parābō. — I’ll make you some chamomile tea.
Paulum mellis adde; sīc dulcius erit. — Add a little honey; it’ll be sweeter.
Exspectā dum refrīgēscat; nimis calidum est. — Wait for it to cool down; it’s too hot.
Fōmentum calidum tibi in pectus impōnam. — I’ll put a warm compress on your chest.
Paulum unguentī tibi illinam. — I’ll put a little ointment on it.
Hīc mentam et serpyllum legāmus, ut domī īnfūsum faciāmus. — Let’s pick mint and wild thyme here, to make tea at home.

blocks.html: Quantities follow L&S: chamaemēlon (Greek χαμαίμηλον), urtīca, serpyllum, hydromeli (short e, Greek ὑδρόμελι). īnfūsum is a Neo-Latin noun (M-O marks it * and writes infûsum); it is written with long ī as in L&S īnfundō, īnfūsus, since in- is long before f.

english: Doctor / medicine / pill / take medicine / prescription / pharmacy / hospital / nurse / dentist
latin: medicus, medicī m. · medicāmentum, medicāmentī n. · pilula, pilulae f.
keywords: doctor GP physician paediatrician medicine medication drug pill tablet capsule lozenge cough drop syrup painkiller prescription pharmacy chemist drugstore hospital clinic nurse dentist ambulance check-up examine visit the doctor

items.html: medicus, medicī m.; medica, medicae f. — doctor (Traupman 63; M-O s.v. doctor; Cic.). medicum arcessere — send for the doctor (Plaut. Men. 875; L&S). Traupman’s sick girl is told Vīse medicum quam prīmum — “see a doctor as soon as possible” (Traupman 55).
medicīna, medicīnae f. — the art of medicine; also a remedy, and the doctor’s surgery (Traupman 63, 166; M-O s.v. doctor’s office, citing Plautus).

medicāmentum, medicāmentī n.; medicāmen, medicāminis n. — medicine, a drug, a remedy (Traupman 63; M-O s.v. drug, medicine; Cic.). M-O gives ingerere for “take” medicine, from 19th-century medical Latin; the plain classical verb is sūmere, as in Seneca’s sopōre sūmptō — “having taken a sleeping draught” (Ep. 83.27).

pilula, pilulae f. — pill (Traupman 59, 65; Plin.); pastillus, pastillī m. — tablet, lozenge (Traupman 66; M-O s.v. pill, tablet, lozenge; Cels.); catapotium, catapotiī n. — pill, a Greek medical word in Celsus and Pliny. Traupman and M-O disagree on which to use for a pill; all three are ancient. pastillus tussiculāris — cough drop (Traupman 63, Neo-Latin); M-O’s cough syrup is syrūpus tussiculāris, with medieval syrūpus.

medicāmentum anōdynum — painkiller (M-O s.v. pain medicine, after Celsus 5.25); Traupman’s plainer phrase: pilula quae dolōrem levābit — “a pill that will ease the pain” (Traupman 57). dolōrem levāre / lēnīre — relieve pain.

praescrībō, praescrībere, praescrīpsī, praescrīptum — prescribe (M-O); medicī praescrīptum — the doctor’s orders (M-O, citing Plin. NH 14.143). Traupman’s prescription: praeceptum medicum (364). aegrum īnspicere — examine a patient (M-O; Plaut. Pers. 316 īnspicere morbum tuum lubet).

medicāmentārius, medicāmentāriī m. — chemist, druggist (Plin. NH 19.110); medicāmentāria, medicāmentāriae f. — pharmacy (Traupman 307, a coinage); pharmacopōlium, pharmacopōliī n. — pharmacy (M-O, modern). In Cicero and Horace a pharmacopōla is a quack, so we don’t use it for the chemist.

valētūdinārium, valētūdināriī n. — hospital (Traupman 64; M-O; Sen., Tac., Cels.); nosocomīum, nosocomīī n. — hospital (M-O; late Latin, Cod. Just.). nosocoma, nosocomae f.; nosocomus, nosocomī m. — nurse (Traupman 65; M-O; late Latin).
medicus dentārius — dentist (Traupman 63; M-O s.v. dentist, a modern phrase).
arcera, arcerae f. — ambulance (Traupman 271; M-O s.v. ambulance, adding automata); in the Twelve Tables and Gellius a covered cart for the sick. Traupman also has autoarcera.
Hodiē ad medicum īmus. — We’re going to the doctor today.
Medicus tē īnspiciet: ōs aperī, linguam exsere. — The doctor will look at you: open your mouth, stick out your tongue.
Hanc pilulam cum aquā sūme. — Take this pill with water.
Medicāmentum amārum est, sed prōderit. — The medicine is bitter, but it’ll do you good.

blocks.html: valētūdinārium: L&S has the adjective valētūdinārius; the neuter noun is in Celsus, Seneca and Tacitus. Lewis & Short gives nosocomīum with long ī (Greek νοσοκομεῖον).

english: Feeling ill: I don’t feel well / fever / sick / feel sick / throw up / tummy ache / headache / sore throat / sneeze
latin: febris, febris f. · aeger, aegra, aegrum · vomō, vomere
keywords: ill sick unwell poorly not feeling well feel better fever temperature hot forehead headache stomach ache tummy ache earache toothache sore throat hoarse sneeze bless you nausea feel sick car sick motion sickness throw up vomit be sick diarrhoea constipated dizzy faint shiver chills

items.html: aeger, aegra, aegrum; aegrōtus, aegrōta, aegrōtum — ill, sick (Traupman 65); aegrōtō, aegrōtāre — be ill. in morbum incidere — fall ill (Traupman 65); morbō corripī — come down with an illness (Traupman 95).
Mē male habeō. / Minus valeō. — I don’t feel well (Traupman 55, 98); Melius mē habeō. / Melius valeō. — I feel better (Traupman 56, 98).

febris, febris f. (acc. febrim or febrem) — fever (Traupman 64; M-O): febrim habēre (Cic. Fam. 7.26.1), in febrim incidere — get a fever (Cic. Fam. 14.8.1). febrīcula, febrīculae f. — a slight temperature (Cic. Att. 12.1.2, of his little daughter Attica: dē Atticae febrīculā … valdē doluī). febrīcitāre — run a fever (Traupman 64; Cels., post-Augustan).
Frōns calida est. — Your forehead is hot (after Traupman 55: frōns et genae sunt calidae).

Venter mihi dolet. / Caput mihi dolet. / Faucēs dolent. — My tummy / head / throat hurts (Traupman 55–56: stomachus dolet; caput dolet; faucēs dolent). Traupman also has dolor stomachī (385) and ā capite labōrāre, have a headache (268). M-O gives tormina, colic (Cic., Plin.), and capitis dolor. aurium dolor — earache (M-O); dentium dolor — toothache (Traupman 396; M-O, citing Cels. 6.9).
raucus, rauca, raucum — hoarse (Traupman 64; Cic.); faucēs asperae — sore throat (M-O); Traupman: exasperātae faucēs (382).

sternuō, sternuere, sternuī — sneeze; sternūmentum, sternūmentī n. — a sneeze (Traupman 65; Cic. Div. 2.84). After a sneeze: Salvē! or Salūtem! (Traupman 94); Pliny notes the custom: cūr sternuentēs salūtāmus? (NH 28.23). Catullus’s blessing: Amor … sternuit approbātiōnem (Catull. 45.8–9).
nausea, nauseae f.; nauseō, nauseāre — nausea; feel sick (M-O; Hor., Cels.); vehentium nausea — car sickness, motion sickness (M-O, a descriptive phrase).
vomō, vomere, vomuī, vomitum — throw up, be sick (Traupman 402; M-O); vomitus, vomitūs m. — vomiting (Plaut.).

alvus fūsa / cita — diarrhoea (Traupman 303); M-O: ventris fluctiō (Plin. NH 23.99). alvum suppressam habēre — be constipated (Traupman 296). crūditās, crūditātis f. — indigestion (Traupman 64; Cic.).
vertīgō, vertīginis f. — dizziness (Traupman 63; M-O; Liv., Plin.); animō linquī — faint (M-O, citing Suet. Caes. 45).
tremō, tremere, tremuī — shiver (Traupman 65); horror febrīlis — a feverish chill (Neo-Latin Lexicon, after Kirsch).
Quid tibi est? Ubi dolet? — What’s wrong? Where does it hurt?
Febrim habēs; hodiē domī manēbimus. — You’ve got a temperature; we’ll stay home today.
Nauseāsne? Dīc mihi, sī vomitūrus es. — Do you feel sick? Tell me if you’re going to throw up.

blocks.html: febris: L&S marks the e as common (fē^bris, “the ē predominating in poets”); the poets’ long scansion may only reflect the heavy syllable before -br-, and de Vaan (s.v. febris) does not discuss the quantity, so the e is left unmarked. febrīcula and febrīcitāre have long ī (L&S).

english: Bumps and scrapes: hurt yourself / bruise / bump / swelling / cut / scab / scar / plaster / bandage / sting / bite
latin: contūsiō, contūsiōnis f. · vulnus, vulneris n. · fascia, fasciae f.
keywords: hurt yourself injury bruise black and blue bump lump swelling swollen cut graze scrape wound bleed blood scab scar plaster band-aid sticking plaster bandage dressing first aid sprain twist ankle broken bone fracture burn insect bite bee sting mosquito lice nits

items.html: Nocuistīne tibi? — Did you hurt yourself? After Traupman 60: Ego mihi nocuī in gymnasiō. noceō, nocēre, nocuī + dative — hurt, harm.

contūsiō, contūsiōnis f. — bruise (Traupman 63; M-O s.v. sprain: bruise; rare, Scribonius); contundō, contundere, contudī, contūsum — bruise (Traupman 63, p. 60 cāsū cecidī et mē contudī); līvor, līvōris m. — a black-and-blue mark (Traupman 62; Plaut.), līvidus, līvida, līvidum — black and blue.
tūber, tūberis n.; tūberculum, tūberculī n. — bump, lump (M-O s.v. bump; Cels.); Traupman has only the verb offendō (see the Trip / slip entry).
tumidus, tumida, tumidum — swollen (Traupman 66; Cic.); tumēscō, tumēscere — swell up (Traupman 61: genū sinistrum tumēscit).

vulnus, vulneris n. — wound, cut (Ter., Cic.); neither source has a headword, Traupman only “bandage a wound”. sanguis, sanguinis m. — blood; cruor, cruōris m. — blood that has flowed from a wound (Traupman 57). Sanguis fluit. — It’s bleeding.
crusta, crustae f. — scab (M-O; Cels. 5.9 ulcerum crusta); cicātrīx, cicātrīcis f. — scar (Ter., Cic.; not in either source).

splēnium, splēniī n. — sticking plaster, a patch (Mart. 2.29.9; Plin. Ep. 6.2.2); emplastrum, emplastrī n. — medical plaster (Cato, Cels.). Comenius: Chīrūrgus cūrat vulnera et ulcera splēniīs (Orbis pictus 128). Traupman has only taenia adhaesīva, adhesive tape (268), and M-O gives no Latin for plaster, so “band-aid” is our application of splēnium.
fascia, fasciae f. — bandage (Traupman 62; Cels.); ligāre, dēligāre — bandage (Traupman 276); fascia gypsea — plaster cast (Neo-Latin Lexicon s.v. plaster cast, after Helfer).
luxō, luxāre — sprain, dislocate (Traupman 65; M-O; Sen., Plin.); Traupman’s noun is luxātūra (late, Marc. Emp.). fractūra, fractūrae f. — fracture (Traupman 64; Cato), os frangere — break a bone.
ambūstiō, ambūstiōnis f.; adūstiō, adūstiōnis f. — a burn (M-O s.v. burn; both Pliny).

acūleus, acūleī m. — sting (Traupman 385; Cic. Tusc. 2.52 apis aculeum); ictus, ictūs m. — bite or sting of an insect (Traupman 280); culex, culicis m. — mosquito, gnat (Traupman 347); pedīculus, pedīculī m. — louse (Traupman 342, printing pēdicul·us; L&S pĕdīculus; Cels.).
Ostende mihi ubi doleat. — Show me where it hurts.
Nihil est; līvor tantum. Fōmentum frīgidum impōnāmus. — It’s nothing, just a bruise. Let’s put a cold compress on it.
Vīsne splēnium? Ecce, jam melius est. — Do you want a plaster? There, that’s better already.

blocks.html: ambūstiō and adūstiō: L&S leaves the u unmarked; the long ū is assumed from ūstus by Lachmann’s rule and should be checked. L&S gives pĕdīculus, short e and long ī, for both the louse and the little foot; Traupman’s pēdiculus is not followed.

items.html: tālus, tālī m. — ankle (Traupman 57); calx, calcis f. — heel (Traupman 58); planta, plantae f.; solum, solī n. — sole of the foot (Traupman 59). ā capite ūsque ad calcem — from head to toe (Traupman 100).
digitus pedis; pollex, pollicis m. — toe; big toe; unguis pedis — toenail (Traupman 59). See the body-parts entry for digitus, pollex.
sūra, sūrae f. — calf (Traupman 57); femur, femoris n. — thigh (Traupman 59); coxa, coxae f. — hip (Traupman 58).
natēs, natium f. — bottom, buttocks (Traupman 57; dV s.v. natis); clūnēs, clūnium m./f. — haunches, rump (Hor., dV).
umbilīcus, umbilīcī m. — belly button, navel (Traupman 57; Cels.).
āla, ālae f.; axilla, axillae f. — armpit (Traupman 57).
supercilium, superciliī n. — eyebrow (Traupman 58; M-O); palpebra, palpebrae f. — eyelid (see the body-parts entry); pūpilla, pūpillae f. — pupil of the eye (Traupman 59; M-O pūpula, both classical).

palpebrae pilus — eyelash (M-O, after Cels. 6.6.15 and Cic. ND 2.143 mūnītaeque sunt palpebrae tamquam vallō pilōrum). Traupman 58 gives cilium for eyelashes, but classically cilium is the eyelid (L&S); M-O says to avoid it.

maxilla, maxillae f. — jaw (Traupman 58); occipitium, occipitiī n. — back of the head (Traupman 58; M-O; Plaut.); vertex, verticis m. — crown of the head (Traupman 58); cervīx, cervīcis f. — nape, neck (Traupman 58).
lacertus, lacertī m. — upper arm (Traupman 57); articulus, articulī m. — joint, knuckle (Traupman 58; Plin.).
costa, costae f. — rib; spīna, spīnae f. — spine, backbone; scapulae, scapulārum f. — shoulder blades (Traupman 59); mūsculus, mūsculī m. — muscle (Traupman 58).
os, ossis n. — bone (Traupman 57); cutis, cutis f. — skin (Traupman 65).

cor, cordis n.; cerebrum, cerebrī n.; pulmōnēs, pulmōnum m.; jecur, jecoris n.; rēnēs, rēnum m.; vēsīca, vēsīcae f. — heart, brain, lungs, liver, kidneys, bladder (Traupman 57–58, spelling jecur with i).
nārēs, nārium f. — nostrils (Traupman 59); nārēs comprimere — hold one’s nose (M-O).
Ubi est umbilīcus tuus? — Where’s your belly button?
Tange calcem, deinde tālum, deinde genū. — Touch your heel, then your ankle, then your knee.

items.html: lentīgō, lentīginis f.; lenticula, lenticulae f. — freckle (M-O s.v. freckle; Cels., Plin.).
naevus, naevī m. — mole, birthmark (Cic. ND 1.79); nota genetīva — birthmark (M-O s.v. birthmark, after Suet. Aug. 80). The Neo-Latin Lexicon gives naevus (Lev.) and naevus māternus (Helfer).
gelasīnus, gelasīnī m. — dimple (M-O s.v. dimple; Mart. 7.25.6) (vōx rāra: Mart.).
rūga, rūgae f. — wrinkle (Traupman 66; Plaut., Hor.); rūgōsus, rūgōsa, rūgōsum — wrinkled.
calvus, calva, calvum — bald; calvitium, calvitiī n. — baldness (Traupman 62; Cic.); capillī mihi dēfluunt — I’m losing my hair (M-O, after Plin. 11.230).

crispus, crispa, crispum; cirrātus, cirrāta, cirrātum — curly (Traupman 58, M-O); cirrus, cirrī m.; cincinnus, cincinnī m. — curl, ringlet. cānus, cāna, cānum — grey-haired (M-O; Plaut., Hor.); flāvus, flāva, flāvum — fair, blond (M-O).
scaeva, scaevae m. — a left-handed person (M-O s.v. left-handed; Dig. 21.1.12); sinistrā manū agiliōre — left-handed (M-O; Suet. Tib. 68).
superiōris labrī barba — moustache (M-O, after Egger). Traupman 58 gives subium, which M-O notes occurs only in a word-list in the grammarian Charisius; M-O’s mystax is Greek, in Jerome.
Lentīginēs habēs, sīcut mamma. — You’ve got freckles, like Mum.

blocks.html: crispus: Traupman marks crīspāre with a long ī, but L&S leaves crispus and crispō unmarked, and no other evidence for a long vowel was found; the i is left unmarked.

english: Gestures and body actions: stretch / hold your breath / blush / wink / sigh / smile / frown / snap your fingers / shake hands
latin: pandiculor, pandiculārī · ērubēscō, ērubēscere · subrīdeō, subrīdēre
keywords: stretch stretching on waking hold your breath breathe in breathe out blush go red wink blink sigh smile grin frown cheer up unknit your brow snap fingers shake hands stand on tiptoe cross-legged pick your nose make a face

items.html: pandiculor, pandiculārī — stretch oneself, as on waking (M-O s.v. stretch; Plaut. Men. 5.2.80 ut pandiculāns ōscitātur — “how he stretches and yawns!”). M-O adds Erasmus’s nervōs distendere.

animam comprimere — hold one’s breath (Ter. Ph. 5.6.28, in L&S: animam compressī, aurem admōvī); M-O’s animam continēre (Cic. de Or. 1.261). spīrāre; īnspīrāre; exspīrāre — breathe; breathe in; breathe out (Traupman 63).
ērubēscō, ērubēscere, ērubuī — blush, go red (Traupman 149; Cic.).
nictō, nictāre — wink, blink (Traupman 407; Plin.).
suspīrō, suspīrāre — sigh (Cic. Att. 2.21.2); Traupman 157 gives gemō, gemere, which is rather to groan.
subrīdeō, subrīdēre, subrīsī — smile (Traupman 158; M-O); M-O also gives arrīdēre, renīdēre.
frontem contrahere — frown, knit the brows (Cic. Clu. 72; Hor.); frontem exporrigere — smooth the brow, cheer up (M-O, citing Vives): Terence exporge frontem — “unknit that brow” (Ad. 839).
ōs dūcere — pull a face (Traupman 97); see also vultum dūcere in the body-parts entry.
digitīs concrepāre — snap one’s fingers (Traupman 98; M-O; Plaut. Mil. 206). dextram jungere cum aliquō — shake hands (Traupman 107; M-O dextrās jungere).
in digitōs ērigī — stand on tiptoe (M-O; Quint. 2.3.8). crūribus dēcussātīs sedēre — sit cross-legged (M-O, a modern phrase). nārēs fodere — pick one’s nose (M-O).
Pandiculāre, sīcut fēlēs! — Stretch, like a cat!
Animam comprime … jam ēmitte! — Hold your breath … now let it out!
Exporge frontem, mī fīlī. — Cheer up, my boy.

english: Waking up and bedtime: stretch / are you awake? / sleepy / dream / nightmare / snore / sleep in / make the bed
latin: vigilō, vigilāre · somnium, somniī n. · stertō, stertere
keywords: awake are you awake wide awake stay up all night sleepy drowsy eyes closing dream dreams what did you dream nightmare bad dream snore snoring sleep in lie in oversleep make the bed time to get up drag out of bed early morning

items.html: vigilō, vigilāre — be awake (Traupman 35, 38): Etiam vigilās? — Vigilō. — Are you awake yet? — I am (Plaut. Most. 383, 373b). pervigilāre — stay awake all night (Traupman 56 noctem pervigilābam).
Tempus est surgere. — Time to get up (Traupman 35). bene māne — very early (Cic. Att. 4.9.2 bene māne haec scrīpsī; Traupman 35 Omnīnō ōdī surgere tam bene māne).
somniculōsus, somniculōsa, somniculōsum — sleepy (Traupman 380; Cordier: Cūr tū es adeō somniculōsus?); oculī somnō cōnīvent — my eyes are closing with sleep (M-O, after Cic. ND 1.82).

somnium, somniī n. — dream (Cic. Div.); somniō, somniāre — dream. Seneca: somnium narrāre vigilantis est — telling a dream is for someone awake (Ep. 53.8). vigilantis somnium — daydream (M-O, after Quint. 6.2.30).

somnium turbulentum — nightmare (Traupman 351); somnium terrificum (M-O, 16th century). Neither has an ancient citation; Ambrose’s hymn prays nec … pavor quiētōs suscitet — that no fright wake us at rest.
stertō, stertere, stertuī — snore (Traupman 381; Cic., Hor.). Erasmus: Nōn tē pudet … in multam lūcem stertere?
somnum in multum diem prōdūcere — sleep in, sleep late (M-O). Horace’s idlers in mediōs dormīre diēs (Ep. 1.2.30).
lectum sternere — make the bed (Traupman 38, 36 mementō sternere lectulum tuum).
ē lectulō extrahere — drag someone out of bed (Traupman 36).
Quid somniāvistī? — What did you dream?
Somnium malum erat; nunc vigilās, et ego hīc sum. — It was a bad dream; now you’re awake, and I’m here.
Audīn’? Avus stertit! — Hear that? Grandpa’s snoring!

blocks.html: Horace Ep. 1.2.30 is quoted from M-O and was not checked against a text.

english: Grooming: hairbrush / hairpin / hair band / curl / fringe / haircut / hairdresser / shave / tweezers / cut your nails
latin: pēniculus comātōrius · tondeō, tondēre · rādō, rādere
keywords: hairbrush hair brush hairpin hair clip hair band headband ribbon curl curls curler curling iron fringe bangs haircut get a haircut hairdresser barber barbershop shave razor tweezers nail clippers cut your nails nail clippings shampoo washcloth flannel toilet paper tissue toothpick gargle mouthwash

items.html: pēniculus comātōrius — hairbrush (Traupman 325; comātōrius, “for the hair”, is Petronius’s word). acus comātōria — hairpin (Traupman 325; Petr. 21.1). taenia, taeniae f.; vitta, vittae f. — hair band, ribbon (Traupman 117; L&S).
crispāre — curl the hair (Traupman 36, 38; M-O capillum crispāre, Plin.); calamister, calamistrī m. — curling iron (Traupman 38; Plaut.).
antiae, antiārum f. — fringe, bangs (Traupman 160; M-O; Apul.).
tondērī — get a haircut (M-O; Liv. 27.34.6); capillum alicui tondēre — cut someone’s hair (M-O; Cic.). Traupman: tōnsūra, facere ut capillus tondeātur (325).
tōnsor, tōnsōris m.; tōnstrīx, tōnstrīcis f. — barber, hairdresser (Traupman 276, 325; M-O); tōnstrīna, tōnstrīnae f. — barbershop (Traupman; Plaut.).
rādō, rādere, rāsī, rāsum — shave; barbam rādere (M-O); Traupman: faciem cotīdiē rāsitāre, shave every day (Suet. Oth. 12). novācula, novāculae f. — razor (Traupman 369; M-O).
volsella, volsellae f. — tweezers (M-O; Plaut., Mart.).
unguēs resecāre — cut one’s nails (Traupman 58); M-O: unguēs praesecāre (Hor. AP 294). Plautus’s miser who collects his barber’s nail clippings, praesegmina (Aul. 312), is a ready story.
lōmentum capillāre — shampoo (Traupman 377); classically lōmentum is a bean-meal face wash (Mart.), so this is a modern extension.
chartula hygiēnica — toilet paper (Traupman 395, modern). dentiscalpium, dentiscalpiī n. — toothpick (Traupman 396; M-O; Mart.).
gargarīzāre — gargle (M-O; Cels.); collūtōrium, collūtōriī n. — mouthwash (Traupman 64; M-O, modern).
Hodiē tondēberis. — You’re having a haircut today.
Dā mihi manum; unguēs tibi resecābō. — Give me your hand; I’ll cut your nails.

blocks.html: Existing entries already cover the comb, nail, toothbrush, soap, towel, hair dryer and mirror; this entry adds the rest of the barber’s and bathroom vocabulary.
